So the card does not teach an effect twice as strong as the source, and the proposed replacement would delete a correct, library-verified figure on a false premise. What survives is the calibration prong the finding also raises: the reviewers' own caveat ('hospital-based studies of limited quality ... true size of effect is likely to be less than demonstrated') is stripped, and 'strongest inpatient numbers' is a ranking Xia never makes — this library's own Therapy on the Unit page (V07) carries the caveat and explicitly warns 'don't quote NNT 5 as though it were precise' (the readmission estimate rests on 206 participants). Corrected finding keeps both NNTs, drops the unlicensed superlative, adds the caveat, and downgrades severity S2 to S3.

Diabetes Care 2004)' (line 838). The 2004 ADA/APA/AACE/NAASO Consensus Development Conference statement (Diabetes Care 2004;27:596-601) schedules the fasting lipid profile at baseline, 12 weeks, then every 5 years — annually is not in the consensus (its annual items are BP, fasting glucose, waist circumference, and family history updates; weight is 4/8/12 weeks then quarterly, which the table renders correctly). The problem is real and precisely scoped: the direction is conservative, but a learner citing 'ADA/APA says annual lipids' would be misquoting the named document, exactly the claim-source mismatch this library's evidence policy targets. The replacement keeps the row accurate to the consensus while noting that annual rechecking is common current practice — correct on both halves and appropriate for both audiences. The embedded quiz (line 804) only tests the 12-week recheck, so it stays correct under the fix.

Quote is verbatim (line 693), and the topic_meta key point repeats it word-for-word at line 631 as the finding states. Per the PubMed abstract of Boggs et al., J Gen Intern Med 2020;35(6):1709-1714 (PMID 32040838, doi:10.1007/s11606-020-05641-4), the study is a quasi-experimental instrumental-variable analysis at Kaiser Permanente Colorado in which the exposure was provider DOCUMENTATION of lethal means assessment (NLP-detected) among patients endorsing suicidal ideation on the PHQ-9, with attempt/death within 180 days falling from 3.3% to 0.83% — so the page's attribution of the result to delivery of 'structured lethal-means counseling (CALM)' misdescribes the exposure, 'cut' overstates a non-randomized design whose authors themselves caution that co-occurring prevention practices may contribute, and the sentence carries no citation. The internal contradiction is verified: the same volume's Therapy on the Unit page states that controlled studies of means-change interventions show 'a small reduction, if any, in deaths' with citation [9] = Shank et al., Inj Prev 2026 (lines 110 and 216). The replacement is faithful to Boggs (quasi-experimental, documented assessment, 0.83% vs 3.3% at 180 days, framed as association rather than randomized effect) and is level-appropriate for MS3s and residents alike.

Quote is verbatim (line 1069), but the claimed problem is not real: per the PubMed abstract of Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022;9(3):211-221 (PMID 35093198, doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00437-5), the network meta-analysis compared 11 family intervention models across 90 RCTs with 10,340 participants, and 'ORs compared with treatment as usual ranged from 0·18 (95% CI 0·12-0·27) for family psychoeducation alone to 0·63 ... for community-based interventions', with the authors concluding family psychoeducation alone 'was superior to the more complex models.' OR 0.18 is therefore the point estimate, not a credible-interval bound or transcription error, and every element of the quoted sentence (0.18, led the 11 models, 90 RCTs, >10,000 patients) is faithful. The reviewer's OR ~0.33 recollection belongs to the companion NMA (Bighelli et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2021;8:969-980, doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00243-1), whose differently-defined nodes gave family interventions OR 0.35, relapse-prevention programmes 0.33, and a family-psychoeducation node of 0.56 — a different analysis. Applying the proposed replacement would make the material wrong. The dependent instances (TL;DR, key point, quiz key, and exp_family's ~37%→~10%, which back-derives correctly from OR 0.18) all stand; the finding's own low confidence anticipated exactly this check, which resolves against it.
